contact_edits.before: O'Haire apart, the best things about the show are the ironic presence of Marni Nixon, the celebrated vocal ghost who dubbed Audrey Hepburn in the Fair Lady film, in the non-singing role of Mrs. Higgins, and the un-ironic excellence with which she plays it. Walter Charles has his moments as Colonel Pickering, though he's too little the gentleman, too much the buffoon. Distressingly further down the same road is Justin Bohon's Freddy, so exaggerated a twit that, though he has the voice to sing On the Street Where You Live, he completely forfeits the right. Anthony Ward's sets make an evocative job of Covent Garden (where the production has its most charming moments) and an imposing one of Higgins' monumentally book-lined study. His establishment is, as usual, impossibly large for a mere professor of phonetics: I counted four maids, two footmen and a housekeeper. Broadway has always been more starry-eyed about the British class system than Britain itself was. Which, though I'm not complaining, is the difference in a nutshell between the incurably romantic My Fair Lady and its impenitently satirical source. - My Fair Lady plays until May 31. For ticket information, call 416-872-1111.
